repairs.value: Strongest feature: Sechler offers a recognizable Lewisian mechanism: heaven and hell express each person’s settled orientation toward God, rendering another person’s destiny nontransferable rather than available for altruistic reassignment. Principal limitation: This mechanism remains stipulated; invoking annihilation, inwardly locked gates, divine perfection, and voluntary separation establishes neither universally informed rejection nor the hypothetical’s evaluative impossibility. Live burden: Sechler needs to demonstrate why individual orientation necessarily precludes substitution while still confronting Clifton’s intended test of whether Christlike love accepts ultimate personal loss for an undeserving beneficiary. Locked score: The 62 appropriately reflects an intelligible eschatological answer whose clarity exceeds its evidential foundation and whose responsiveness diminishes because it dissolves rather than answers the scenario’s sacrificial challenge.

Strongest feature: Clifton repairs Sechler’s impossibility objection by defining substitution as the hypothetical test itself, then grounding its intelligibility in Christianity’s admiration of Christlike self-surrender for undeserving beneficiaries. Principal limitation: The analogy remains conditional and incomplete; an expressly invented opportunity cannot establish afterlife possibilities, while Christ’s temporary descent and redemptive role differ from a human’s permanent forfeiture of heaven. Live burden: Clifton needs to explain why those differences preserve sufficient structural similarity and why imagined willingness reveals anything consequential about divine hiddenness or real postmortem incentives. Locked score: The 77 appropriately reflects exceptional responsiveness, clear calibration, and substantial burden relevance, tempered by limited evidential warrant and an analogy whose theological correspondence remains suggestive rather than demonstrated.
